title: Pregnancy loss, stillbirth and end of life care
blurb: Offer the right birth options after an intrauterine death, give compassionate care to the National Bereavement Care Pathway standards, and explain how the baby's death will be reviewed.
question: A woman at 36 weeks is found to have an intrauterine fetal death. She is well, her membranes are intact and there are no signs of infection or bleeding. What should the midwife and obstetrician do about the birth?

teach.body: SPM 4.11 asks midwives to work with interdisciplinary and multiagency teams to give respectful, kind, compassionate end of life care to the woman and her newborn, partner and family, and to follow up with the family, ensuring continuity of care. In plain English: when a baby dies, the midwife's job is not over. She gives the woman real choices, protects time with the baby, and makes sure the family is not lost between services afterwards.

teach.body: The NBCP is an improvement programme so that every bereaved family gets consistently high-quality, compassionate, personalised care. It has pathways for miscarriage (including ectopic and molar pregnancy), termination for fetal anomaly, stillbirth, neonatal death and sudden unexpected death in infancy. Its nine standards cover a parent-led care plan, a proper bereavement room, memory making, emotional and mental health support, clear signalling of the loss, involvement in reviews, staffing, training and staff support.

teach.caption: A bereavement room should not be used for other purposes, and parents should not have to pass families with live babies.

teach.caption: MNSI also takes babies with suspected severe brain injury and maternal deaths (England).

teach.body: Grace, 38 weeks, is told her baby has died. She is well and her membranes are intact. Midwife Leanne and the obstetrician explain expectant management, induction or caesarean and give her time; Grace chooses induction tomorrow. Leanne gives one-to-one care in labour in the bereavement suite, offers time with Isla, photographs and hand prints, explains the review her care will receive and that Grace can contribute, and makes sure the GP and health visitor are told.

teach.text: Do not rush every woman to immediate induction. Immediate birth is offered when there are ruptured membranes, infection or bleeding. If she is well with intact membranes, she chooses between expectant management, induction and caesarean.

items: Signal the bereavement on paper and electronic records so no one asks about the baby.
Inform the GP, health visitor and community midwife before discharge.
Offer emotional support and referral for specialist mental health support if needed.
Explain the review, name a key contact and arrange follow-up to discuss findings.
Plan trauma-informed support in any future pregnancy.
Well, intact membranes, no infection or bleeding: discuss expectant, induction or caesarean and respect her choice (NG207 1.2.28).
Ruptured membranes, infection or bleeding: offer immediate induction or caesarean (1.2.29).
Induction: mifepristone 200 mg then a prostaglandin, or mechanical; one-to-one midwifery care in labour.
NBCP: five pathways and nine standards, from bereavement rooms to staff support.
PMRT reviews deaths from 22 weeks to 28 days; parents are told and can contribute.

summary: You can now offer the right birth options after an intrauterine fetal death and give bereavement care in line with the National Bereavement Care Pathway. You can also explain to parents how their baby's death will be reviewed and how they can take part.

A.q: A woman at 37 weeks has a confirmed intrauterine fetal death. Her membranes have ruptured and she has a temperature of 38.4 °C. What should be offered?
options: Expectant management for up to 48 hours
Immediate induction of labour or caesarean
Discussion of all options over the next week
Oral antibiotics and a review in 24 hours
A.why: NG207 1.2.29: with ruptured membranes, infection or bleeding, offer immediate induction of labour or caesarean birth.

whyNot.0: Expectant management is not appropriate with ruptured membranes and infection.
whyNot.2: Delay is unsafe when there is evidence of infection.
whyNot.3: Infection with a fetal death needs birth to be offered now, not oral antibiotics and review.

A.q: A woman with an intrauterine fetal death and an unscarred uterus chooses induction. Which first medicine does NICE recommend?
A.why: NG207 1.2.31: offer oral mifepristone 200 mg followed by vaginal dinoprostone or oral or vaginal misoprostol, or a mechanical method.

whyNot.0: An oxytocin infusion is not the recommended first agent for IUFD induction.
whyNot.1: Dinoprostone is the second step, given after mifepristone.
whyNot.2: Misoprostol is the second step, given after mifepristone.

A.q: Which of these is one of the five National Bereavement Care Pathway pathways?
A.why: The NBCP pathways are miscarriage, termination for fetal anomaly, stillbirth, neonatal death and sudden unexpected death in infancy.

whyNot.1: Maternal death is not one of the five NBCP pathways.
whyNot.2: Hyperemesis is a pregnancy complication, not a bereavement pathway.
whyNot.3: Postnatal depression is a mental health condition, not an NBCP pathway.

B.q: A woman is in labour after an intrauterine fetal death at 34 weeks. What level of midwifery care does NICE recommend?
options: Care led by the obstetric registrar
B.why: NG207 1.2.30: if a woman with an IUFD chooses induced labour, provide one-to-one midwifery care during labour and birth.

whyNot.0: Shared care falls below the one-to-one standard.
whyNot.1: She needs one-to-one midwifery care; the obstetric team works alongside it.
whyNot.3: Hourly checks are not continuous one-to-one care.

B.q: After a stillbirth at 30 weeks, the parents ask whether anyone will look at what happened. What should the midwife explain?
options: A review happens if they make a complaint
A local review will happen, with their input
No review is held for babies under 37 weeks
The coroner will review every stillbirth
B.why: PMRT supports reviews of all baby deaths from 22 weeks; parents are told a review will happen and how they can contribute.

whyNot.0: The review happens whether or not they complain.
whyNot.2: PMRT reviews baby deaths from 22 weeks, so a stillbirth at 30 weeks is reviewed.
whyNot.3: Stillbirths are not routinely reviewed by the coroner; the PMRT review is the usual hospital review.

B.q: Parents of a stillborn baby are being cared for on the labour ward. Which arrangement best meets the NBCP standards?
options: A side room on the postnatal ward
A bereavement room used for this purpose
A bay screened from other families
B.why: NBCP standard 2: access to an appropriate bereavement room that is not used for other purposes, where parents do not pass or hear families with live babies.

whyNot.0: On a postnatal ward they would hear babies and other families.
whyNot.1: A routine delivery room may expose them to other births and is not designed for bereavement.
whyNot.3: A screened bay gives no privacy from families with live babies.

C.q: A woman with an intrauterine fetal death at 39 weeks had a caesarean in her last pregnancy. She asks about induction. What must the discussion include?
options: Induction is not possible after a caesarean
Prostaglandins carry a risk of uterine rupture
Expectant management is not an option for her
Caesarean birth has no long-term effects
C.why: NG207 1.2.32: discuss that induction can lead to uterine rupture and that dinoprostone and misoprostol licences contraindicate their use with a uterine scar, plus mechanical methods and the risks of caesarean.

whyNot.0: Induction is possible; she needs information on methods and risks to choose.
whyNot.2: If well with intact membranes, expectant management remains an option to discuss.
whyNot.3: NICE says to discuss the short- and long-term morbidity of caesarean birth.

C.q: A baby dies on day 3 after a term labour in an English trust. Besides the local review, which body must the trust notify?
C.why: MNSI investigates early neonatal deaths (0 to 6 days) of babies born after labour at 37 weeks or more; trusts in England must notify these events.

whyNot.1: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not investigate baby deaths.
whyNot.2: The HSE deals with workplace health and safety, not maternity investigations.
whyNot.3: The NBCP is a care improvement programme, not an investigating body.

C.q: Two weeks after a neonatal death, a mother attends the antenatal clinic for her GP letter and a receptionist congratulates her on the birth. Which NBCP standard has failed?
C.why: NBCP standard 5: a system clearly signals to all staff that a parent has been bereaved, through paper and electronic records and local protocols.

whyNot.0: The bereavement room standard concerns where care is given around the loss.
whyNot.1: Memory making concerns time and support with the baby.
whyNot.2: The learning standard concerns reviews and involving parents in them.

reteach.title: Choice, time and follow-through
reteach.question: What three things should every bereaved woman get from her midwife?

blocks.body: Choice: if she is physically well with intact membranes, she decides on expectant management, induction or caesarean. Time: a private bereavement room, one-to-one care, memory making at her pace. Follow-through: records signal the loss, community teams are told, and she hears how her baby's death will be reviewed and how to take part.

blocks.text: The conditions that remove the choice are ruptured membranes, infection or bleeding. Without them, it is her decision.

explain.body: If the woman is physically well with intact membranes and no infection or bleeding, discuss expectant management, induction or caesarean and respect her choice.

test.q: A woman is well with intact membranes after an intrauterine fetal death at 32 weeks. She wants to go home for a day before deciding. What is the best response?
options: Insist on induction before she leaves
Support her decision and agree a plan
test.why: NG207 1.2.28: discuss the options and respect the woman's decision when she is well with intact membranes and no infection or bleeding.

whyNot.0: Induction is an option, not a requirement, in this situation.
whyNot.1: Caesarean is one option but is not indicated urgently here.
whyNot.3: Admission is not needed if she is well; she may choose expectant management.

explain.body: NBCP standard 3: support parents to make memories, with enough time and space, and protocols so parents can take their baby outside the hospital if they wish.

test.q: Parents of a stillborn baby ask whether they can take their baby home before the funeral. What should the midwife do?
options: Tell them babies must stay in the mortuary
Advise them to ask the funeral director
Follow the local protocol to support them
Refer the request to the coroner
test.why: NBCP standard 3: protocols for taking babies outside the hospital should be in place and staff confident to support parents to do so.

whyNot.0: The NBCP expects services to support this choice.
whyNot.1: The midwife should support the request rather than pass it on.
whyNot.3: The NBCP expects a local protocol to support this, not a coroner referral.

explain.body: The Perinatal Mortality Review Tool supports standardised, multidisciplinary local reviews of baby deaths from 22 weeks, including late miscarriages, stillbirths and neonatal deaths. Care is graded and parents receive a plain-language explanation.

test.q: From what gestation does the Perinatal Mortality Review Tool cover baby deaths?
test.why: PMRT supports review of baby deaths from 22 weeks' gestation, including late miscarriages, stillbirths and neonatal deaths.

whyNot.0: 20 weeks is earlier than the PMRT threshold.
whyNot.1: 24 weeks is later than the PMRT threshold.
whyNot.2: 28 weeks is later than the PMRT threshold.

explain.body: NBCP standards 8 and 9: mandatory bereavement care training with annual refreshers, post-mortem consent training for anyone discussing post-mortem, and staff wellbeing prioritised with a trauma-informed approach.

test.q: A newly qualified midwife is asked to discuss post-mortem options with bereaved parents. According to the NBCP standards, what must she have completed?
test.why: NBCP standard 8: all staff who speak with parents about post-mortem options must have completed post-mortem consent training.

whyNot.1: A counselling diploma is not the NBCP requirement.
whyNot.2: Preceptorship is general support, not the specific training required.
whyNot.3: Life support training is unrelated to post-mortem consent.
